definition: A reagent is a substance added to take part in a chemical reaction — combined, changed, or used up as the reaction runs, most often to test what a sample contains.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word reagent. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know reagent should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: One drop of the iodine reagent turned the potato slice blue-black, betraying the starch hidden inside.
Ingredient is weaker than reagent — an ingredient only has to be present in the mix, while a reagent is added precisely so that a chemical reaction will happen.
Accelerant goes further than reagent — a reagent starts or steers a reaction at a working pace, while an accelerant whips one into racing, often destructive speed.

A catalyst speeds a reaction up but comes out unchanged on the other side, ready to work again. A reagent is a working participant: it gets used up, combined, or transformed by the reaction it drives.

An indicator is the narrow specialist — a substance whose whole job is to signal, usually by a color change, that something is present. Reagent is the broader working word for any substance added to take part in a reaction, whether it signals, dissolves, or builds.

The stream-monitoring volunteers unpacked a rack of small bottles at each bend of the creek, one reagent for every question they meant to put to the water.
A few drops of the first in a vial of creek water blushed pink: nitrates.

By the fourth test the team had a chemical portrait of the river, drawn one reagent at a time.

Reagent is bench vocabulary: use it for a substance added to make a chemical reaction go, especially in a test.
A kitchen has ingredients; a lab has reagents — swap the two words in either direction and the sentence sounds wrong.
Keep the working family straight: a catalyst speeds the reaction but comes out unchanged, an indicator only signals, and the reagent is the participant that gets used up doing the job.
And this unit's prefix is hiding in plain sight: a reagent is literally a re-agent, the agent you add so the sample will act back.

On water-testing day, each team gets a vial of pale-yellow reagent and a row of samples drawn from the creek.
Two drops go into every tube.
Where the water carries dissolved iron, the liquid combines with it — and in doing so, the reagent itself is changed and used up.
By the eighth sample the vial is visibly emptier, which is the point: a substance that takes part in a reaction gets spent by it.
The teacher contrasts it with the glass stirring rod, which touches every sample and comes out exactly as it went in.
At the end, teams log their results and hand back their vials — most of them nearly dry.
